projectCategory: DSA Module 1.2: Linked List Data Structures & Pointer Mechanics
subject: Data Structures & Algorithms in C

projects.title: Singly Linked List Creation & Dynamic Head Insertion Engine
projects.description: Unlike standard arrays that require contiguous physical memory blocks, a Linked List stores data in discrete dynamic nodes scattered across heap memory. Each node consists of two parts: a data payload and a pointer holding the memory address of the next node. In this project, you will build a foundational Singly Linked List in C. You will write an O(1) head insertion function (`insert_at_head`) using dynamic memory allocation (`malloc`). When inserting a new value, your code allocates a node struct, populates its data field, points its `next` pointer to the current `head`, and updates `head` to point to the new node. You will also write a traversal function to display the node chain and a memory release function (`free_list`) that systematically frees every heap node to prevent memory leaks.
projects.learningOutcome: Heap Node Allocation (malloc), Pointer Manipulation & O(1) Head Insertion
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Singly Linked List Head Insertion ---
Head → [10 | next] → [20 | next] → [30 | next] → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Node Allocation**: Allocate dynamic node memory `(Node*)malloc(sizeof(Node))`.
2. **Pointer Relinking**: Set `new_node->next = head`.
3. **Head Update**: Set `head = new_node` to complete insertion in O(1) time.
4. **Heap Cleanup**: Traverse list using a temporary pointer and call `free()` on every node.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `insert_at_head()`: Allocates new node, points its next to head, and returns new head pointer.
2. `print_list()`: Iterates through node chain printing value and pointer links.
3. `free_list()`: Releases heap memory for all nodes sequentially.

projects.title: Singly Linked List Traversal, Node Counting & Memory Address Printer
projects.description: Because linked list nodes are allocated dynamically on the heap, consecutive nodes are usually NOT stored in contiguous memory addresses! In this project, you will build a diagnostic Linked List Inspector. Your application traverses a Singly Linked List from `head` to `NULL`, counting the total number of nodes while printing the hexadecimal RAM memory address of each node (`%p`), its internal integer payload, and the address stored in its `next` pointer. This provides physical insight into non-contiguous heap allocation, pointer dereferencing, and boundary checking (`while (curr != NULL)`).
projects.learningOutcome: Non-Contiguous Heap Layout Inspection, Pointer Dereferencing & Node Counting
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Node Memory Layout Inspection ---
Node 1: Value=100, RAM Address=0x55e4b2, Next Address=0x55e4c8
Node 2: Value=200, RAM Address=0x55e4c8, Next Address=0x55e4e0
Node 3: Value=300, RAM Address=0x55e4e0, Next Address=(nil)
Total Node Count = 3
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Traversal Loop**: Initialize `curr = head`, loop while `curr != NULL`.
2. **Address Formatter**: Print `curr->data`, `(void*)curr` (node RAM location), and `(void*)curr->next`.
3. **Counter Increment**: Increment node count at each iteration.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `count_nodes_and_print_memory()`: Iterates through nodes, printing memory pointers and counting total elements.

projects.title: Tail Insertion & Appending Engine with O(1) Tail Pointer Tracking
projects.description: Inserting an element at the end (tail) of a Singly Linked List normally requires traversing from `head` all the way to the last node, taking O(N) time. However, in queue implementations and append-heavy data structures, we maintain a secondary `tail` pointer pointing directly to the last node. In this project, you will construct a Singly Linked List with Dual Pointer Tracking (`head` and `tail`). When appending a new node, if the list is empty, both `head` and `tail` point to the new node. If the list is non-empty, you link `tail->next = new_node` and update `tail = new_node` instantly in O(1) constant time without traversing the list!
projects.learningOutcome: Head & Tail Dual Pointer Management, Appending Mechanics & O(1) Tail Insertion
projects.exampleOutput:
--- O(1) Tail Insertion Engine ---
List: 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Dual Pointer Struct**: Maintain `head` and `tail` pointers inside a `LinkedList` structure.
2. **Empty Case**: If `head == NULL`, set both `head = new_node` and `tail = new_node`.
3. **Non-Empty Append**: Set `tail->next = new_node`, then update `tail = new_node`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `append_tail()`: Appends new node at the end in O(1) time using tail pointer.

projects.title: Node Deletion by Key with Safe Pointer Relinking & Memory Cleanup
projects.description: Deleting a specific value from a Singly Linked List requires finding the target node, updating the previous node's `next` pointer to bypass the target node, and freeing the target node's memory. In this project, you will implement a Key-Based Node Deletion Engine in C. Your code handles three distinct scenarios: (1) empty list, (2) deleting the `head` node (which requires updating `head = head->next`), and (3) deleting a middle or trailing node by tracking `curr->next->data == key`. You will enforce strict memory safety by saving the target node pointer into a temporary variable `temp` before unlinking, calling `free(temp)` to eliminate memory leaks.
projects.learningOutcome: Node Deletion Logic, Head Replacement, Pointer Relinking & Zero-Leak Memory Freeing
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Node Deletion by Key ---
Before: 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL
After Deleting 20: 10 → 30 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Head Match**: If `head->data == key`, save `temp = head`, update `head = head->next`, and `free(temp)`.
2. **Middle Match**: Search with `curr->next->data == key`, set `temp = curr->next`, update `curr->next = curr->next->next`, and `free(temp)`.
3. **Key Not Found**: If target is missing, return list unchanged.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `delete_by_key()`: Locates target key, relinks surrounding pointers, and frees node memory.

projects.title: Doubly Linked List Creation & Bi-Directional Traversal Engine
projects.description: A Doubly Linked List (DLL) enhances Singly Linked Lists by giving each node two pointers: `next` (pointing forward) and `prev` (pointing backward). This enables bi-directional traversal (forward and reverse) and O(1) deletion when a node pointer is given. In this project, you will construct a Doubly Linked List in C. Each `DNode` contains `data`, `DNode *prev`, and `DNode *next`. You will write a head insertion function that properly updates both forward (`next`) and backward (`prev`) pointer links, followed by a dual traversal routine that prints the list forward from `head` to `tail` and backward from `tail` to `head`.
projects.learningOutcome: Doubly Linked List Architecture, Dual Pointer Links & Bi-Directional Traversal
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Doubly Linked List Bi-Directional Traversal ---
Forward : 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 <-> NULL
Backward: 30 <-> 20 <-> 10 <-> NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Node Struct**: Node contains `data`, `struct DNode *prev`, `struct DNode *next`.
2. **Head Link Update**: Set `new_node->next = head`, `new_node->prev = NULL`. If `head != NULL`, set `head->prev = new_node`.
3. **Reverse Traversal**: Walk to tail using `next` pointer, then walk back to head using `prev` pointer.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `insert_doubly_head()`: Inserts node at head updating both prev and next pointers.
2. `print_bidirectional()`: Prints forward and reverse traversals.

projects.title: Doubly Linked List In-Place Head & Tail Insertion
projects.description: Building a full Doubly Linked List container requires maintaining both `head` and `tail` boundary pointers for instant O(1) push_front and push_back operations. In this project, you will build a Doubly Linked List Container in C supporting both `push_front` and `push_back`. You will ensure that when inserting into an empty list, both `head` and `tail` point to the single new node. When pushing to the front or back of an existing list, both forward (`next`) and backward (`prev`) links of adjacent nodes are correctly updated without breaking structural integrity.
projects.learningOutcome: Doubly Linked List Head/Tail Boundary Management, Push Front & Push Back
projects.exampleText: Push Front 20, Push Front 10, Push Back 30
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Doubly Linked List Head & Tail Insertion ---
List: 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 <-> NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Push Front**: Set `n->next = head`. If `head` exists, `head->prev = n`; else `tail = n`. Update `head = n`.
2. **Push Back**: Set `n->prev = tail`. If `tail` exists, `tail->next = n`; else `head = n`. Update `tail = n`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `push_front()` & `push_back()`: Perform O(1) front and back insertions on doubly linked list.

projects.title: Circular Singly Linked List Creation & Round-Robin Traversal
projects.description: In a Circular Linked List, the `next` pointer of the final node points back to the `head` node instead of `NULL`, forming a continuous loop. Circular linked lists are widely used in operating system CPU round-robin scheduling, audio buffer looping, and multiplayer turn-taking games. In this project, you will implement a Circular Singly Linked List in C. You will write an insertion function that maintains the tail-to-head circular reference (`tail->next = head`) and write a round-robin traversal function that loops through the list a specified number of full cycles.
projects.learningOutcome: Circular Pointer Topologies, Round-Robin Looping & Eliminating NULL Terminated Boundaries
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Circular Singly Linked List Simulation ---
Circular Traversal (2 rounds): 10 → 20 → 30 → 10 → 20 → 30 → (loop continues...)
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Single Node Case**: If `head == NULL`, node points to itself (`n->next = n`).
2. **Circular Linkage**: Locate last node (`curr->next == head`), set `curr->next = n` and `n->next = head`.
3. **Loop Traversal**: Traverse `curr = curr->next` and track full rotations when `curr == head`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `insert_circular()`: Maintains tail-to-head circular pointer.
2. `print_circular()`: Demonstrates multi-round circular traversal.

projects.title: Search Key in Linked List with Pointer Position Tracking
projects.description: Unlike arrays where element access by index `i` is O(1), searching for a target value in a Linked List requires sequential linear traversal (O(N) time) starting from `head`. In this project, you will construct a Key Search Engine for Singly Linked Lists. Your program iterates through nodes using a position counter (`pos = 0`). If a node's data matches `key`, the function returns its zero-based index position. If the search reaches `NULL` without finding the key, it returns `-1`. You will test the search engine with both existing and non-existing search keys.
projects.learningOutcome: Sequential Search on Linked Structures, Index Position Tracking & Target Matching
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Key Search Engine ---
Key 25 found at zero-based index: 1
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Linear Search Loop**: Loop `curr` from `head` while `curr != NULL`.
2. **Match Check**: If `curr->data == key`, return `pos`.
3. **Not Found**: If loop finishes without match, return `-1`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `search_key()`: Scans linked list sequentially and returns zero-based index of target key.

projects.title: Find Middle Node of Singly Linked List (Fast & Slow Pointer Technique)
projects.description: Finding the middle node of a Singly Linked List in a single pass is a classic algorithm problem. A two-pass approach first counts total nodes N and then iterates N/2 steps. But using Floyd's Fast & Slow Pointer Technique (Tortoise and Hare), you can find the middle node in a SINGLE pass! In this project, you will implement Fast & Slow Pointers in C. Initialize `slow = head` and `fast = head`. Advance `slow` by 1 step (`slow = slow->next`) and `fast` by 2 steps (`fast = fast->next->next`). When `fast` reaches the end (`NULL` or `fast->next == NULL`), `slow` is guaranteed to be pointing exactly at the middle node!
projects.learningOutcome: Fast & Slow Pointer (Tortoise & Hare) Pattern, Single-Pass Middle Node Finding
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Fast & Slow Pointer Middle Finder ---
List: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → 50 → NULL
Middle Node Value = 30
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Two Pointers**: `slow` moves 1 node per iteration, `fast` moves 2 nodes.
2. **Speed Ratio**: Because `fast` travels twice as fast, when `fast` reaches end, `slow` is at `N/2`.
3. **Single Pass**: Solves problem in O(N) time and O(1) space in one pass.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `find_middle()`: Uses fast and slow pointers to locate center node in a single pass.

projects.title: Delete Linked List Node at Position K with Memory Deallocation
projects.description: In contrast to deleting by key value, deleting a node at zero-based index position K requires navigating to index `K - 1` and updating its `next` pointer to point to index `K + 1`. In this project, you will build a Position-Based Node Deletion Engine in C. You will handle boundary conditions including: (1) invalid position K < 0 or out of bounds, (2) K = 0 (head node deletion), and (3) valid position K > 0 (traversing K-1 steps, relinking `curr->next = curr->next->next`, and freeing position K node).
projects.learningOutcome: Position-Based Pointer Navigation, Index Boundary Safety & Node Freeing
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Delete Node at Position K ---
Before: 5 → 15 → 25 → NULL
After deleting pos 1: 5 → 25 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Head Case (K=0)**: Save `temp = head`, update `head = head->next`, `free(temp)`.
2. **Position Navigation**: Loop `curr` K-1 steps. If `curr` and `curr->next` exist, set `temp = curr->next`, update `curr->next = curr->next->next`, `free(temp)`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `delete_at_position()`: Navigates to position K-1, relinks pointers, and frees position K node.

projects.title: In-Place Singly Linked List Reversal (Iterative 3-Pointer Approach)
projects.description: Reversing a Singly Linked List in-place (reversing all `next` pointers so that the list flows from tail to head) is one of the most fundamental data structure operations. Creating a new reversed list doubles memory consumption. The optimal solution uses the Iterative 3-Pointer Technique. In this project, you will implement 3-Pointer List Reversal in C using `prev`, `curr`, and `next`. Initialize `prev = NULL`, `curr = head`. In a `while (curr != NULL)` loop: save `next = curr->next`, reverse link `curr->next = prev`, advance `prev = curr`, and advance `curr = next`. When the loop finishes, `prev` is the new `head` pointer!
projects.learningOutcome: Iterative 3-Pointer In-Place Reversal, Pointer Re-direction & O(1) Auxiliary Memory
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Iterative List Reversal (3-Pointer) ---
Before: 1 → 2 → 3 → NULL
Reversed: 3 → 2 → 1 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Three Pointers**: `prev = NULL`, `curr = head`, `next = NULL`.
2. **Pointer Reversal Loop**: Save `next = curr->next`, flip `curr->next = prev`, advance `prev = curr`, advance `curr = next`.
3. **New Head**: Return `prev` as new head pointer.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `reverse_iterative()`: Reverses all pointer direction links in-place in O(N) time.

projects.title: Recursive Singly Linked List Reversal Engine
projects.description: While iterative reversal uses explicit loops, list reversal can also be solved elegantly using Recursion! In this project, you will implement Recursive Linked List Reversal in C. The base case returns `head` if `head == NULL` or `head->next == NULL`. In the recursive step, call `new_head = reverse_recursive(head->next)`. To reverse the link between `head` and its successor, set `head->next->next = head` and break the old forward link with `head->next = NULL`. The function returns `new_head` up the call stack.
projects.learningOutcome: Recursive Call Stack Unwinding, Base Cases & Implicit Backtracking Pointer Reversal
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Recursive List Reversal ---
Before: 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL
Reversed: 30 → 20 → 10 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Base Case**: If `!head || !head->next`, return `head`.
2. **Recursive Call**: `new_head = reverse_recursive(head->next)`.
3. **Link Inversion**: Set `head->next->next = head` and `head->next = NULL`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `reverse_recursive()`: Uses call stack unwinding to reverse list links recursively.

projects.title: Detect Cycle in Linked List (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare Algorithm)
projects.description: A corrupt linked list can contain a cycle where a node's `next` pointer points back to a previously visited node, causing infinite traversal loops! Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare) detects cycles in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space. In this project, you will implement Floyd's Cycle Detection in C. Maintain `slow` and `fast` pointers starting at `head`. Move `slow` by 1 node and `fast` by 2 nodes per step. If a cycle exists, `fast` will enter the loop, catch up to `slow` from behind, and eventually `slow == fast`. If `fast` or `fast->next` reaches `NULL`, no cycle exists.
projects.learningOutcome: Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm, Mathematical Relative Velocity & Loop Identification
projects.exampleText: List with cyclic node connection n3 → n1
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Floyd's Cycle Detection ---
Cycle Detected in Linked List!
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Pointer Speed Difference**: `slow` speed = 1, `fast` speed = 2.
2. **Relative Speed**: In a loop of length C, distance between fast and slow decreases by 1 cell every step.
3. **Intersection Guarantee**: `fast` must meet `slow` if cycle exists.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `detect_cycle()`: Runs Tortoise & Hare algorithm to check for infinite pointer loops.

projects.title: Find Cycle Starting Node in Linked List (Mathematical Proof Engine)
projects.description: Detecting a cycle is only half the battle; real-world memory allocators and deadlock detectors need to find the EXACT node where the cycle begins! In this project, you will implement Cycle Start Node Detection in C based on Floyd's mathematical theorem. Phase 1 runs standard cycle detection until `slow` and `fast` meet at intersection node `K`. Phase 2 resets an `entry` pointer to `head` while keeping `slow` at `K`. Advance both `entry` and `slow` by 1 step simultaneously: the node where they meet is mathematically proven to be the exact cycle starting node!
projects.learningOutcome: Floyd's Mathematical Cycle Proof, Pointer Alignment & Exact Loop Entry Finding
projects.exampleText: Cyclic List where n4 points to n2
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Cycle Start Node Finder ---
Cycle starts at Node with Value = 20
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Mathematical Invariant**: Distance from `head` to cycle start equals distance from intersection point `K` to cycle start.
2. **Dual Step Traversal**: Reset `entry = head`. Advance `entry` and `slow` 1 step at a time.
3. **Meeting Point**: `entry == slow` yields the exact cycle entry node.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `find_cycle_start()`: Implements Phase 1 intersection and Phase 2 entry alignment to locate cycle start.

projects.title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists into Single Sorted Linked List
projects.description: Given two pre-sorted linked lists L1 and L2, combine them into a single sorted linked list in linear O(N + M) time without allocating new node data structures. In this project, you will build a Sorted List Merging Engine in C. You will use a dummy head node `dummy` and a `tail` pointer. In a `while (l1 != NULL && l2 != NULL)` loop, compare `l1->data` and `l2->data`, attach the smaller node to `tail->next`, and advance `l1` or `l2`. Once one list is exhausted, attach the remaining chain to `tail->next`.
projects.learningOutcome: Dummy Head Node Pattern, In-Place Node Splicing & MergeSort Sub-step
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Merge Two Sorted Lists ---
Merged: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Dummy Node**: Simplifies edge case handling for head pointer initialization.
2. **Pointer Comparison**: Compare `l1->data` vs `l2->data`, attach smaller node to `tail->next`.
3. **Remaining Splice**: Attach leftover non-null list directly in O(1) time.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `merge_two_sorted()`: Splices pre-sorted linked lists into a single sorted chain.

projects.title: Check if Singly Linked List is Palindrome (Half Reversal Method)
projects.description: A linked list is a Palindrome if its node values read the same forward and backward (e.g., [1 → 2 → 2 → 1]). Checking this in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space without copying to an array requires a multi-step technique. In this project, you will implement Palindrome Detection in C: (1) use Fast & Slow pointers to find the middle node, (2) reverse the second half of the linked list in-place, (3) compare elements of the first half and reversed second half node-by-node, and (4) restore the second half back to original order.
projects.learningOutcome: Multi-Step Algorithm Composition, In-Place Half Reversal & Palindrome Testing
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Palindrome Linked List Test ---
List is a Palindrome!
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Find Middle**: Fast & Slow pointers locate middle node.
2. **Reverse Half**: Invert `next` links of second half in-place.
3. **Compare**: Compare first half vs reversed second half for value equality.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `is_palindrome()`: Uses middle node finding and half list reversal to test palindrome property.

projects.title: Remove Duplicates from Unsorted Linked List using Hash / Nested Loops
projects.description: Removing duplicate values from an UNSORTED linked list requires finding all recurring numbers and freeing their nodes. While a sorted list can remove duplicates in O(N) time, an unsorted list requires tracking visited values. In this project, you will implement an Unsorted Duplicate Remover in C using two pointer runners (`curr` and `runner`). For each node `curr`, `runner` scans all downstream nodes (`runner->next`); whenever `runner->next->data == curr->data`, the duplicate node is unlinked and freed in O(N^2) time and O(1) space.
projects.learningOutcome: Nested Pointer Runner Pattern, Unsorted Duplicate Cleanup & Dynamic Memory Management
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Remove Duplicates from Unsorted List ---
Before: 10 → 20 → 10 → 30 → NULL
After : 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Outer Loop**: `curr` iterates from head to end.
2. **Inner Runner**: `runner` checks `runner->next` against `curr->data`.
3. **Unlink Duplicate**: Set `temp = runner->next`, `runner->next = temp->next`, `free(temp)`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `remove_duplicates_unsorted()`: Removes duplicate nodes from unsorted list using runner pointers.

projects.title: Intersection Point of Two Linked Lists (Y-Shaped Linked List)
projects.description: Suppose two separate Singly Linked Lists (List A and List B) merge at a common node, forming a Y-shaped structure. How do you find the exact intersecting node memory address in O(N + M) time and O(1) space? In this project, you will build an Intersection Finder in C using the Two-Pointer Traversal Swapping Technique. Initialize `pA = headA` and `pB = headB`. Advance both pointers 1 step at a time. When `pA` reaches `NULL`, redirect it to `headB`; when `pB` reaches `NULL`, redirect it to `headA`. Because both pointers traverse `Len(A) + Len(B)` nodes total, they will hit the exact intersecting node at the exact same step!
projects.learningOutcome: Y-Shaped Linked List Topologies, Two-Pointer Length Equalization & Intersection Finding
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Intersection Point of Two Linked Lists ---
Intersection Node Value = 8
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Length Equalization**: Redirecting `pA` to `headB` and `pB` to `headA` forces both pointers to travel identical distance `M + N`.
2. **Convergence Guarantee**: `pA` and `pB` meet at intersecting node or `NULL` simultaneously.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `get_intersection()`: Equalizes traversal paths to find Y-shaped list intersection.

projects.title: N-th Node from End of Linked List (Two-Pointer Offset Strategy)
projects.description: Finding the N-th node from the end of a Singly Linked List in a single pass without knowing the list length requires the Two-Pointer Offset Strategy. In this project, you will implement N-th From End Finder in C. Initialize `fast = head` and `slow = head`. Advance `fast` pointer N steps forward. Then, move both `fast` and `slow` forward 1 step at a time. When `fast` reaches `NULL`, `slow` is positioned exactly at the N-th node from the end!
projects.learningOutcome: Two-Pointer Offset Window, Single-Pass Tail Counting & Boundary Validation
projects.exampleOutput:
--- N-th Node from End (Two-Pointer Offset) ---
List: 10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → NULL
The 2-nd node from end = 30
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Advance Fast**: Move `fast` N steps ahead of `slow`.
2. **Simultaneous Traversal**: Advance `fast` and `slow` until `fast == NULL`.
3. **Offset Invariant**: Gap of N nodes guarantees `slow` lands at N-th node from end.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `find_nth_from_end()`: Uses N-step pointer offset window to locate node from tail.

projects.title: Doubly Linked List Node Deletion with Dual Pointer Relinking
projects.description: Deleting a given target node `del` from a Doubly Linked List is faster than in a Singly Linked List because `del` already contains a direct pointer to its predecessor (`del->prev`). In this project, you will implement Doubly Linked List Node Deletion in C. You will handle four boundary cases: (1) empty list or NULL node, (2) deleting `head` (`head = del->next`), (3) updating predecessor (`del->prev->next = del->next`), and (4) updating successor (`del->next->prev = del->prev`). You will carefully free `del` memory.
projects.learningOutcome: Doubly Linked List Node Deletion, Dual Link Cleanup & Head/Tail Re-assignment
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Doubly Linked List Node Deletion ---
Before: 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 <-> NULL
After deleting node 20: 10 <-> 30 <-> NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Head Case**: If `del == head`, set `head = del->next`.
2. **Link Fixes**: If `del->next`, set `del->next->prev = del->prev`. If `del->prev`, set `del->prev->next = del->next`.
3. **Free Memory**: `free(del)`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `delete_doubly_node()`: Relinks forward and backward pointers around deleted node.

projects.title: Reverse Nodes in K-Group (Grouped Reversal Engine)
projects.description: Given a Singly Linked List, reverse the nodes of the list K at a time and return its modified list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of K, left-over nodes at the end remain in original order. In this project, you will build a K-Group Reversal Engine in C. First, check if at least K nodes exist downstream. If yes, reverse K nodes using iterative pointer reversal and recursively link `head->next = reverse_k_group(next, k)`. If fewer than K nodes remain, return `head` without reversing.
projects.learningOutcome: K-Group Segmented Reversal, Hybrid Iterative-Recursive Relinking & Subsegment Management
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Reverse Nodes in K-Group (K=2) ---
Before: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → NULL
After : 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5 → NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Count K Nodes**: Verify at least K nodes exist.
2. **K-Node In-Place Reversal**: Reverse K nodes using 3 pointers.
3. **Recursive Stitching**: Link tail of reversed segment to result of next K-group recursive call.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `reverse_k_group()`: Performs segmented K-group list reversal recursively.

projects.title: Flattening a Multi-Level Doubly Linked List with Child Pointers
projects.description: Suppose you have a Doubly Linked List where nodes can have a `child` pointer pointing to a separate sub-level doubly linked list. Flatten the multi-level structure into a single 1D doubly linked list where all nodes appear in depth-first order. In this project, you will build a Multi-Level Flattening Engine in C. As you traverse nodes, whenever `curr->child` is non-NULL, locate the tail of the child list, splice the child list between `curr` and `curr->next`, update `prev`/`next` links, and clear `curr->child = NULL`.
projects.learningOutcome: Multi-Level Hierarchical Structures, Depth-First Splicing & Complex Pointer Relinking
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Flatten Multi-Level Doubly Linked List ---
1 <-> 3 <-> 2 <-> NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Child Detection**: When `curr->child != NULL`, find tail of child branch.
2. **Splice Branch**: Set `child_tail->next = curr->next`, `curr->next = curr->child`, `curr->child->prev = curr`.
3. **Clear Child**: Set `curr->child = NULL`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `flatten_multi_level()`: Flattens multi-level child branches into a single 1D list.

projects.title: Copy Linked List with Arbitrary/Random Pointers (Interleaving Technique)
projects.description: Given a linked list where each node contains an extra `random` pointer pointing to any arbitrary node in the list or `NULL`, create a deep copy of the list. Doing this in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space without a hash table requires the Interleaving Technique. In this project, you will implement Deep Copy with Random Pointers in C: (1) insert cloned nodes immediately after original nodes (`orig->next = clone`), (2) assign `clone->random = orig->random->next`, and (3) separate interleaved lists back into original and cloned lists.
projects.learningOutcome: Deep Copying Graph-Like Topologies, Interleaved Node Splicing & O(1) Space Cloning
projects.exampleText: Copy list with random pointer cross-links
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Copy List with Random Pointers (Interleaving) ---
Clone Node 1: Val=10, Random Val=20
Clone Node 2: Val=20, Random Val=10
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Interleave**: Duplicate each node `A → A' → B → B'`.
2. **Random Copy**: `curr->next->random = curr->random->next`.
3. **Unweave**: Separate original nodes and cloned nodes into independent chains.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `copy_random_list()`: Uses 3-pass interleaving technique to clone random pointer lists in O(1) space.

projects.title: Memory-Efficient XOR Doubly Linked List (Bitwise Pointer Compression)
projects.description: Standard Doubly Linked Lists require TWO pointers per node (`prev` and `next`), taking 16 bytes of pointer overhead on 64-bit systems. An XOR Doubly Linked List compresses both pointers into a single pointer field `npx` storing the bitwise XOR address: `npx = Address(prev) ^ Address(next)`. In this project, you will build an XOR Doubly Linked List in C. Using uintptr_t casting and the bitwise XOR operator (`^`), you will write insertion and traversal routines that compute the next node address dynamically using `next = XOR(prev, curr->npx)`, reducing memory overhead by 50%!
projects.learningOutcome: Bitwise XOR Pointer Compression, uintptr_t Type Casting & Memory Overhead Reduction
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Memory-Efficient XOR Doubly Linked List ---
XOR List Forward: 10 <-> 20 <-> 30 <-> NULL
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **XOR Formula**: `npx = prev ^ next`.
2. **Forward Step**: `next = prev ^ curr->npx`.
3. **Backward Step**: `prev = next ^ curr->npx`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `insert_xor()` & `print_xor()`: Implements XOR pointer arithmetic for 50% pointer memory compression.

projects.title: Fixed-Size Linked List Memory Pool Allocator (Zero-Fragmentation Custom Malloc)
projects.description: Frequent `malloc()` and `free()` calls cause heap memory fragmentation and allocation latency. Embedded systems and high-frequency trading platforms pre-allocate a fixed contiguous memory pool array and manage node allocation using an internal free list. In this project, you will build a Custom Fixed-Size Memory Pool Allocator for Linked Lists in C. Your pool initializes a static node array and chains unallocated nodes into a free list. `pool_alloc()` pops a node from the free list in O(1) time without calling OS `malloc()`, and `pool_free()` pushes freed nodes back to the free list in O(1) time.
projects.learningOutcome: Custom Memory Managers, Pre-Allocated Pool Arenas & Zero-Fragmentation Allocation
projects.exampleText: Allocate 2 nodes from pre-allocated memory pool
projects.exampleOutput:
--- Fixed-Size Custom Memory Pool Allocator ---
Allocated Node 1 Val=100 at RAM 0x7fff80
Allocated Node 2 Val=200 at RAM 0x7fff90
Freed nodes back to custom pool successfully!
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Pool Arena**: Declare static array `Node memory[POOL_SIZE]`.
2. **Free List Chain**: Initialize `free_list` linking all free slots.
3. **O(1) Alloc & Free**: Pop/push nodes from `free_list` without calling system `malloc`.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `init_pool()`, `pool_alloc()`, `pool_free()`: Implements custom high-performance zero-fragmentation memory pool.
